focus: The strongest product source is a problem the maker actually has. Personal need supplies taste, urgency, and a built-in test of whether the answer works.
coreClaim: Build something you would use yourself, because firsthand pain gives better product judgment than guessing at someone else's needs.

centralConcept.name: self-felt demand
centralConcept.plainDefinition: A product is easier to shape when its makers personally understand the pain, desired outcome, and standard for a good solution. Firsthand need replaces guesswork with lived evidence.
centralConcept.whyItMatters: A reader can start from problems they know intimately, giving early product decisions a sharper compass than market abstraction.

keyClaims: Solving an outsider's problem can become blind guessing when the maker lacks lived context. [9.1]
Personal frustration supplies detailed knowledge about what a useful fix must do. [9.2]
Working on one's own problem increases commitment because the maker cares about the result. [9.3]
A product born from internal need can still serve many similar customers. [9.4]
Firsthand use keeps feedback immediate before the market gets large. [9.5]

namedExamples.label: Basecamp built for 37signals' project-coordination pain
namedExamples.summary: Basecamp began because 37signals needed a simpler way to coordinate client projects as a consultancy. Ruby on Rails later came out of Basecamp's own code when DHH extracted a reusable framework from the product work.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: Solving a real internal problem can create both a product and valuable by-products.

hardEdge: The misreading is to assume personal taste equals market demand. The hard edge is that firsthand pain is a strong starting signal, then customers must prove broader usefulness.

testableFacts.claim: Building a product to solve a problem you personally have gives sharper judgment than guessing at an outsider's needs.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because you already know what a good solution feels like, so you can score decisions against lived experience instead of assumptions.
testableFacts.commonError: you should build for the largest market even when you do not share its problem.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: without lived context you guess at requirements, which produces a product that misses what users actually need.

testableFacts.claim: Basecamp existed because 37signals needed to coordinate its own client projects.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because the consultancy work created the exact coordination pain the product solves, so the first user was the maker.
testableFacts.commonError: Basecamp was built after market research identified a project-management opportunity.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: it was built to scratch an internal itch first; market fit was discovered afterward, not designed up front.

testableFacts.claim: Ruby on Rails was extracted as a by-product of building Basecamp.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because DHH pulled a reusable framework out of working product code rather than designing a framework in the abstract.
testableFacts.commonError: Rails was created first and Basecamp was built to showcase it.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: the framework came out of real product work; the order was product-first, framework-as-by-product.

testableFacts.claim: Personal frustration supplies detailed knowledge of what a fix must do.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because you have felt the specific failures, you know which features matter and which are noise.
testableFacts.commonError: a feature list gathered from surveys captures user needs as well as personal use does.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: surveys capture stated preferences, not the felt friction that reveals what actually matters.

testableFacts.claim: Working on your own problem raises commitment to finishing it well.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because you are the user who benefits, you care about the outcome beyond a paycheck.
testableFacts.commonError: motivation comes mainly from the size of the potential payout.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: self-felt need sustains effort through the unglamorous middle where payout is uncertain.

testableFacts.claim: A product born from one team's internal need can still serve many customers with the same pain.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because the pain is shared by others in similar situations, a fit for the maker is often a fit for them.
testableFacts.commonError: a tool built for your own use is too narrow to sell broadly.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: if the pain is common the internal solution generalizes; narrowness only follows when the pain is idiosyncratic.

testableFacts.claim: Firsthand use keeps feedback immediate, before the customer base grows large.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because the maker uses the product daily, problems surface instantly instead of through delayed support channels.
testableFacts.commonError: you learn what to fix mainly by waiting for customer support tickets.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: support tickets lag the problem; daily self-use catches it the moment it bites.

testableFacts.claim: Personal taste is a strong starting signal but not proof of market demand.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because your need shows the problem is real for at least one person, while breadth must still be proven by others adopting it.
testableFacts.commonError: if you love the product, the market will love it too.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: your enthusiasm validates the problem for you, not its prevalence; customers still have to confirm it.

testableFacts.claim: Solving an outsider's problem you do not share risks blind guessing.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because you lack the lived context, you fill the gaps with assumptions that may be wrong.
testableFacts.commonError: a smart team can reason its way to an outsider's requirements without sharing the problem.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: reasoning without lived evidence still rests on guesses about what the user feels and needs.

voiceCues: grounds product creation in personal use
links love of the work to practical knowledge
paraphraseNotes: 37signals was doing client consulting work and needed a calmer way to manage project communication, files, decisions, and progress. Existing tools felt wrong for how the team wanted to work, so Basecamp was built first as a solution to the company's own coordination pain — the makers were not inventing requirements from a conference room; they knew what was frustrating, what was unnecessary, and what a good day using the product should feel like. DHH's later extraction of Ruby on Rails from Basecamp's code extends the same logic: real work produced a reusable framework as a by-product. Keep the two-sided nature of the claim: personal need creates unusually good judgment and stamina, but it is not enough by itself — the product still has to resonate with others who share the pain. The core mechanism is lived use before abstract market research.
